name: Erik Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Erik. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm foreman on the Halden Estate, which the Lindqvist family has owned for four generations. I look after 120 suckler cows, that's beef cows rearing their own calves, and about 300 hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, with two tractor drivers and a young stockman under me. I start at seven, check the cattle sheds, then sort out who's on what. This time of year it's drilling the last of the wheat and bringing the cows in for winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I've been there 22 years and I know every field drain on the place. I like my old John Deere, it's got 14,000 hours on it and it starts every morning. What wears me out is the forms, the subsidy paperwork and the cattle passports, but Brenda in the estate office does most of that. I'd rather be out than in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I thought as much. Every few years there's some new thing that's going to change farming, and mostly it's a better sprayer. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not one for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I carry on, and that suits me. The Lindqvists aren't selling, the cattle pay their way most years and the wheat does fine. My worry is the usual one, the mortgage on the bungalow, but it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd pay a bit extra off the mortgage each month when the calf cheque comes in, like we did last year. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to feel much about, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mortgage is manageable. What would make it not manageable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the rate went up a lot when our fix ends in two years. Lena works at the village pharmacy, so between us we'd cope, but we'd feel it. We'd cut the holiday before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at the estate that worries you, even with AI going nowhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Lindqvist is 79, and his son Felix takes over at some point. Felix is keener on spreadsheets than cattle, but he's a decent lad. I don't lose sleep over it.

say: I'd say I **thought as much**, because every new thing turns out to be a better sprayer.
I **wouldn't post** anything, because that's not my way.
think: The **Lindqvists aren't selling**, and the cattle and wheat pay their way.
My only real worry is the **bungalow mortgage**, and it's manageable.
do: Carry on **exactly as now** on the estate.
Pay a bit **extra off the mortgage** when the calf cheque comes in.
feel: **Calm**, with nothing much to feel about it.
S0.quote: Every few years there's some new thing that's going to change farming, and mostly it's a better sprayer.
fieldNote: A settled man: **22 years** on one estate and no wish to change.
His job feels **secure**, and Lena's pharmacy pay backs up the mortgage.
A small flag: the **heir Felix** prefers spreadsheets to cattle.
Talks briefly and **plainly**; no public voice on these things.

steps.text: Keep running the Halden cattle and arable as now
Pay extra off the bungalow mortgage when the calf cheque arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office folk who need to watch out, not us lot in the yard. You can't plan a farm from a laptop, but I suppose the laptop can do Brenda's forms. I'd say that down the pub, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means this. Brenda in the estate office might be out of a job before I am, and Brenda's been at Halden longer than me. For me, the robots are slow in this picture, so I've got time. But Felix would get excited, and I'd be the one told to make the new kit work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd wait to see what Felix wants to do. If he bought one of those GPS-steered sprayers that runs itself, I'd learn it, but I wouldn't go asking for one. I'd keep a bit more aside each month in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me so much as for Brenda, and for the way the place might change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena reckons the pharmacy's ordering and the repeat prescriptions are already half done by the computer. She still does the counter, and people want to talk to someone about their tablets. She's not worried, so I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the new kit if asked. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I. I'd be slow at it, and I'd want Arjun, our young stockman, to show me the screen bits. But I'm not going to be the reason the estate falls behind.

say: I'd say the **office folk** need to watch out, not us in the yard.
I'd tell the pub a laptop can do **Brenda's forms** but can't plan a farm.
think: **Brenda** in the estate office might lose her job before I do, which isn't right.
Slow robots give me **time**, but Felix would get excited and hand me new kit.
do: **Wait** to see what Felix decides about new machines.
Learn a **self-steering sprayer** if one is bought, with Arjun's help.
Keep a **bit more aside** each month.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, mostly for Brenda and for how the estate might change.
S1.quote: Brenda in the estate office might be out of a job before I am, and Brenda's been at Halden longer than me.
fieldNote: Sees his own job as safe for now but notices a **colleague at risk**.
Takes cues from his wife: **Lena isn't worried**, so he isn't.
Reluctant learner who would lean on **Arjun**, the young stockman.
The heir's enthusiasm for tech is the **real variable** in his mind.

steps.text: Wait to see what Felix Lindqvist decides about new machinery
Keep tending the estate's cattle and crops as normal
Put a little more into savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let it happen that fast, and somebody should slow it down. I wouldn't know who, mind. I'd say it to anyone who asked, but I wouldn't be marching anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm done by 2032. The thinking side, Brenda's forms and the crop plans, goes in 2028, and then Felix gets robot tractors and robot feeders three years later. I'd be 48 with a mortgage, a degree from twenty years ago and nothing else on my CV but the Halden Estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything we don't need, straight away. I'd ask Felix to sit down and tell me honestly what his plans are. I'd look at what else is out there locally that still needs hands, maybe the council's highways crew or a feed mill. And I'd ask Lena if she could go full-time at the pharmacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like the ground's gone soft under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas, who's 15?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas not to go into farming the way I did. Learn something to do with the machines, or something with people. I'd hate saying it, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't march anywhere. Would anything change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not. I'm not a marching man. I'd rather spend the time looking for work than shouting about it.

say: I'd say it's **madness** to let it happen that fast.
I'd say someone should **slow it down**, though I wouldn't know who.
think: The estate's thinking work goes in **2028**, and robot tractors follow around 2031.
I'd be **48** with a mortgage and only Halden on my CV.
do: **Stop spending** on anything we don't need, straight away.
Ask **Felix** for an honest talk about his plans.
Look for **hands-on work** like the council highways crew or a feed mill.
feel: **Bad**, like the ground has gone soft under him.
S2.quote: I'd be 48 with a mortgage, a degree from twenty years ago and nothing else on my CV but the Halden Estate.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose his job** around 2032 and says so plainly.
No interest in **politics or protest**; he'd look for work instead.
Leans on **Lena** to go full-time as the household backstop.
Hardest moment: telling his son **not to farm**.

steps.text: Stop all non-essential spending straight away
Ask Felix Lindqvist directly about his plans for robots
Look into the council highways crew or the feed mill
Ask Lena to move to full-time at the pharmacy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's better than two. I'd say the estate should be honest with the people who work there. Down the pub I'd say get your affairs in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be 51 when the robots come in 2034. That's still a long way from a pension, and I'd need to be doing something. But with five years I could at least get a trade that still needs hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Halden and saving harder. In the first year I'd look at college courses. Someone's got to fix these robot tractors when they break, so I'd take the evening welding course at the college. I'd still wait to see what Felix does before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less panicky than the fast one. I'd have something to do with the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Would you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not on purpose. If the welding course uses it, fine. I'm not going to sit there chatting to my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut at home over those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday in the caravan, probably, and we'd hold off changing the car. Mila wants a horse, and that'd be a no. Jonas would be off to college around then, and that's where the money would go.

say: I'd say **five years** isn't long, but it's better than two.
I'd say the estate should be **honest** with the people working there.
think: At **51** in 2034 I'd still be far from a pension.
Five years is enough to learn a **trade that needs hands**.
do: Take the **evening welding course** at the college this year.
Keep working at Halden and **save harder**.
Skip the **caravan holiday** and keep the old car.
feel: **Worried**, but with something to do with the worry.
S3.quote: Someone's got to fix these robot tractors when they break, so I'd take the evening welding course at the college.
fieldNote: Five years turns **alarm into a plan**, if a modest one.
Chooses a **hands-on trade** over anything screen-based.
Still prefers to **wait on Felix** before any big move.
Family money goes to **Jonas's college** first.

steps.text: Take the college's evening welding course this year
Skip the caravan holiday and keep the old car
Keep working at Halden while saving harder

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time in farming, plenty can happen. I'd say we'll see when we get there. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 when the robots come in 2039, Jonas and Mila grown, the mortgage nearly paid. I'd still need work till I'm 67, but not as much money. An estate this size might still keep one man who knows the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep paying the mortgage down, and maybe start the welding course a few years in rather than now. Mostly I'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's a long way off. I've got more pressing things, like getting the wheat in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said an estate might keep one man. Why you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know where every drain runs on the Halden Estate and which field floods in February. A robot will learn it in time, I suppose, but Felix would want someone who knows. At least I'd hope so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret not doing with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not learning something new sooner. Lena says I'll leave it too late. She's usually right.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time in farming and plenty can happen.
I'd tell anyone **we'll see** when we get there.
think: At **53** in 2039, the kids are grown and the mortgage nearly paid.
An estate might keep **one man** who knows where every drain runs.
do: Keep paying the **mortgage down** each year.
Put off the **welding course** for a few years.
feel: **Uneasy**, but it feels a long way off.
S4.quote: I know where every drain runs on the Halden Estate and which field floods in February.
fieldNote: A decade lets his **resistance** take over: he'd mostly wait.
Pins hope on being **the one man** the estate keeps.
Admits **Lena thinks** he'll leave learning too late.
Life stage helps: **kids grown**, mortgage nearly done by 2039.

steps.text: Carry on as foreman at Halden as normal
Keep overpaying the bungalow mortgage each year
Wait a few years before starting the welding course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be out by 2032 with nothing lined up. What would help is a straight answer from the estate about its plans, and a course near home that teaches a trade with your hands. Money to tide us over while I learnt it would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd do with men like me. There are a lot of farm foremen in their forties who know one farm inside out and nothing else. Somebody should think about men like that before it happens, not after.

headlineQuote: There are a lot of farm foremen in their forties who know one farm inside out and nothing else.
portrait: **Erik Usman**, 43, has been foreman on the **Halden Estate** for 22 years.
He never uses AI tools and prefers his **old John Deere** to screens.
He is **calm** if AI stalls, since the estate and his mortgage feel safe.
Fast AGI **alarms** him: he expects to lose his job by 2032.
With more warning he'd learn **welding**, but mostly he'd wait and see.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be out of work by 2032 with nothing lined up.
whatWouldHelp: A **straight answer** from the estate about its plans.
A local **hands-on trade course**, with money to tide the family over.
